The PR says tie-breaking by id keeps paging with --limit stable, but no offset or paging flag exists. --limit only caps the row count, so the stated paging rationale is not delivered by this change.
attacks.evidence: "Ties are broken by transaction id so paging with --limit stays stable." / ABSENT: no --offset or paging flag in the diff

attacks.claim: Test coverage is thin. The desc path is only exercised for amount, so date, payee, and category DESC are untested. The category key is never tested, and the default key is not checked.
attacks.evidence: {key: "amount", desc: true, want: "ORDER BY t.amount_cents DESC, t.id DESC"} is the only desc case; "category" is absent from the cases

attacks.claim: strings.Contains on the query text would still pass if extra or misplaced clauses followed the ORDER BY, and it does not check the LIMIT or WHERE clauses. The tests are also coupled to exact whitespace and clause ordering, and they never run the query against the database to confirm ordering or tie-breaking.

The motivating request asks for sorting by amount or payee, but the PR also ships a category sort key with a join-dependent expression. No cited request covers it, so it extends the public CLI surface without a stated need.
attacks.evidence: "Users asked to sort transaction listings by amount or payee instead of only by posting date." vs. "category": "COALESCE(c.name, '') COLLATE NOCASE"

attacks.claim: Amount sorting uses the raw signed value with ASC by default, so the most negative amounts come first. Neither the help text nor the PR states the sign convention, so users may not know how to get the largest spends at the top.
attacks.evidence: "amount": "t.amount_cents" with dir defaulting to "ASC"; ABSENT: help text or docs for the sign convention

attacks.claim: Sorting by amount, payee, or category has no supporting index, so each call sorts all matching rows before applying LIMIT. Cost grows with the account's transaction count. This is unlikely to matter at current single-user size.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no CREATE INDEX or query-plan check for t.amount_cents, t.payee, or c.name in the diff

attacks.claim: Sort keys are case-sensitive, so --sort Amount or --sort PAYEE fails even though the intent is clear. The error lists only lowercase keys and gives no hint about the mismatch.

Sort expressions hardcode the t. and c. aliases from the surrounding SELECT. Renaming an alias or changing the join will silently break sorting, and nothing ties the map to the query text it is spliced into.
attacks.evidence: "date": "t.posted_at", ... "FROM transactions t LEFT JOIN categories c ON c.id = t.category_id"
